o: Apply m sequential 'replace value a with value b' operations to a distinct-valued array. Because values stay distinct and each replacement target doesn't yet exist, we can treat values themselves as keys: maintain a map from value → its index in nums, and rewrite both the array slot and the map on each operation. Example 2 chains 1→3→2 and 2→1, ending [2,1]. Scanning the array per operation would be O(nm) = 1e10, so hashing is essential.
k: Values act as stable identities across operations; a value→index hash map turns each operation into O(1).
Operations must be applied strictly in order — later ops refer to values produced by earlier ones.

a.i: Build pos[value] = index once. For each operation (a, b): write b into nums[pos[a]], record pos[b] = pos[a], erase pos[a]. Distinctness guarantees no aliasing.
s: Build the value→index map from nums.
Process operations in order, updating the array entry and remapping the index.
a.t: O(n + m) — one build pass plus O(1) average per operation.

a.n: Approach 2: Reverse Pass with Final-Value Mapping
a.i: Process operations right-to-left: first time a value appears as a source, record its ultimate destination; sources never seen again map to themselves. Then rewrite nums once. Same complexity, but demonstrates the 'resolve chains backwards' technique.
s: Walk operations from last to first; maintain dest map: when seeing (a,b), set dest[a] = dest.getOrDefault(b, b).
a.t: O(n + m) — reverse pass plus one rewrite pass.

w: The forward hash-map approach is the most natural; the reverse mapping is elegant if asked to avoid mutating during iteration. Pitfalls: erasing stale keys (or equivalently overwriting them — safe here only because values remain distinct), and assuming you can sort operations. Follow-up: what if replacements could collide (values not guaranteed distinct)?
